newsitem.title: USA: Car collector's list highlights convertibles.
newsitem.headline: Car collector's list highlights convertibles.

text.p: If you love old convertibles, Rick Cole may have a car for you.
Cole, the owner of a California company that auctions collectible cars, has just released the 1997 "Gold List" -- his picks of good values in the market -- and it is chock full of convertibles.
The collector also seems to be focusing on younger and less affluent collectors -- all the cars on the list are less than $30,000 and half can be found for $10,000 or less.
"Convertibles have always been the most desirable of any model," Cole said in a telephone interview. "There's an old saying, 'When the top goes down, the price goes up.'"

"Convertibles are hot stuff," agreed Ronnie Craig at Duffy's Collectible Cars in Cedar Rapids, Iowa (319 364-7000). Fewer are made than other models and new convertibles are expensive compared to regular models, he said.
"The nostalgia thing is huge," Craig said. "People are buying these cars for the juice, the memories they get from when they were younger."

The cars on Cole's list are the ones he expects to appreciate over the next five years. The list is released ahead of the annual Monterey Sports and Classic Car auction to be held Aug. 15-16 in Monterey, Calif. The Rick Cole Auction Co. will offer about 180 cars during the two-day auction.

High on Cole's list are Volkswagen Beetle convertibles from the 1960s and 1970s, which he says are currently worth $6,000 to $7,000 in excellent condition. Cole said he expects next year's introduction of a new VW Bug to boost interest in the original models.

Other convertibles on the list include Pontiac Bonnevilles from the mid-1960s, available for $10,000 to $11,000, Ford Thunderbird models from 1964 through 1966 ($14,000 to $17,000) and early 1960s Lincoln Continentals ($15,000 to $16,000).
T-Birds especially have been known and loved by collectors for their classic lines and styling.

Experts said it is worth doing your homework before buying. Small differences in quality or parts can have a big effect on a car's value. If you're planning to buy and restore an old car, examine it carefully for things such as original parts, colour and other items, which may require the help of experts who know what they're looking for.

Other vehicles on Cole's list include high-horsepower "muscle cars" like the 1969 Plymouth Road Runner ($9,000 to $15,000) and the 1968 Dodge Charger ($7,000 to $10,000), Chevy pickup trucks from the late '60s and early '70s ($5,000 to $10,000) and a 308 GTB Ferrari ($25,000 to $30,000).
Craig from Duffy's said muscle cars in particular were still in big demand.
Emotions aside, people buy old cars to make money. But car prices, which rose astronomically in the 1980s, have become far less predictable.
Taking older cars out for short spins is a good idea to keep them running smoothly, experts said. But the most expensive, heavily restored cars are usually not driven.
Some experts called lists such as Cole's self-serving since they may reflect what an auctioneer is trying to sell.
"They're trying to drum up enthusiasm for certain cars and they're not really sophisticated about it," said one industry veteran, who asked not to be identified.

Asked if the list was meant to drum up sales at the auction, Cole said, "No, not at all. Monterey has nothing to do with these types of cars." He said the average price of a car sold at the auction would be about $80,000 this year.
"Monterey is really a different market," he said. "I've never made a nickel off of Cole's list.

Convertibles to be offered at the Monterey auction include a Maserati 4.9 Ghibli Spyder, estimated to sell for about $100,000, and a Ferrari 500TR Spyder that should fetch $500,000, "easy," Cole said. And the Ferrari needs work, too.
In addition to Cole's and Duffy's, Dean Kruse of Auburn, Ind., also publishes collectible car lists and runs auctions around the country. The phone number is 219 925-5600.
Rick Cole Auction Co. may be reached at 619 350-0800.
